report:
You are correct: **regular intake of vitamin C does not prevent colds** for the general population. Here is the evidence:

**The Cochrane Review (the gold standard)** analyzed 29 trial comparisons involving 11,306 participants and found that regular ingestion of vitamin C (≥200 mg/day) had **no effect on common cold incidence** in the ordinary population. This large body of placebo-controlled trials is the strongest evidence available.

**One exception:** In people under extreme physical stress (marathon runners, skiers, soldiers in sub-arctic conditions), vitamin C supplementation roughly **halved** cold risk. This benefit does not extend to the general public.

**What vitamin C does modestly help:** Regular supplementation slightly **shortens cold duration** — by about 8% in adults and 14% in children — and may reduce severity by about 15%. However, starting vitamin C *after* symptoms begin shows no clear benefit.

**Historical context:** The myth originates with Nobel laureate Linus Pauling, whose 1970 book *Vitamin C and the Common Cold* popularized megadosing. Subsequent large-scale trials failed to confirm his claims, and experts now consider routine mega-dose prophylaxis unjustified for community use.

**Bottom line:** For most people, daily vitamin C will not stop you from catching colds. It may modestly reduce how long a cold lasts if taken regularly, but the preventive benefit is essentially zero outside of extreme physical stress conditions.

**Sources:**
- Cochrane Review: https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD000980_vitamin-c-preventing-and-treating-common-cold
- Cochrane Library (full text): https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD000980.pub4/full
- InformedHealth.org (NCBI): https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK279544/
- Linus Pauling Institute, Oregon State University: https://lpi.oregonstate.edu/mic/health-disease/common-cold
